gloss: nose, nostrils; face; anger; be angry
summary: The nose, the organ of breath: into man's nostrils Yahweh breathed the breath of life (Gen 2:7), and the dual אַפַּיִם is the face, bowed “nostrils to the ground” in homage and worship. From the snorting, burning nose comes anger: “his nose burned” is the Hebrew for “he was angry”, the word scripture uses most for the anger of Yahweh, and Proverbs plays on both senses: “pressing the nose brings out blood, and pressing the nostrils brings out strife” (Pro 30:33). Yahweh is “long of nostrils”, slow to anger, yet there is a day of his anger. The verb אָנֵף is to be angry, almost always of God; Arabic, where to grow “hot in the nose” is to be enraged, and Moabite, where Kemosh “was angry” (יאנף) with his land, show the same tie of nose and anger.

words.summary: About 275 times as a noun, the singular and the dual אַפַּיִם. The bodily sense, the nose and its breath, runs under the whole word: the face is the nostrils bowed to the ground, and anger is the burning, snorting nose. The brief's count of 409 also takes in the conjunction אַף “also, even”, which shares the spelling but is not this word (see the entry's note).

senses.definition: The nose of man or beast, the organ of breath and smell, which can wear a ring, take a hook, or be cut off.

evidence.note: Of idols: “ears they have, and do not hear; אַף they have, and do not smell.”
“A ring of gold in the אַף of a swine is a fair woman without discretion.”
“Pressing milk brings out curds, pressing the אַף brings out blood, and pressing the אַפַּיִם brings out strife”: the nose and anger in one saying.
“I put a ring on your אַף and earrings in your ears.”
Among the finery of the daughters of Zion, “the rings and the nose-rings (נִזְמֵי הָאַף)”.
To Sennacherib: “I will put my hook in your אַף and my bridle in your lips, and turn you back.”
Of Behemoth: “with snares can one pierce his אַף?”
“Your אַף is like the tower of Lebanon, looking toward Damascus.”
“They shall take away your אַף and your ears”: mutilation of the captive.
Flesh to eat “until it comes out of your nostrils (מֵאַפְּכֶם) and is loathsome to you”.
“I made the stench of your camps come up even into your nostrils (וּבְאַפְּכֶם).”

senses.gloss: nostrils as the seat of breath and life
senses.definition: The nostrils as where the breath of life is: God breathes it in, and while it is there a man lives. Of God, the “breath of his nostrils” is the blast of his power and anger.

evidence.note: Yahweh God “breathed into his nostrils (בְּאַפָּיו) the breath of life, and the man became a living soul”.
In the flood “all in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, of all that was on the dry land, died”: man and beast alike.
“Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils (בְּאַפּוֹ), for of what account is he?”
“All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God in my nostrils.”
“The breath of our nostrils, the anointed of Yahweh, was taken in their pits”: the king as the people's very life.
Quotes Gen 2:7: “the first man Adam became a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit.”
“By the breath of your nostrils (וּבְרוּחַ אַפֶּיךָ) the waters were heaped up”: the wind at the sea as God's breath.
“Smoke went up from his nostrils, and fire from his mouth devoured” (also Psa 18:9).
The foundations of the world were laid bare “at the rebuke of Yahweh, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils” (also Psa 18:16).
“By the breath of God they perish, and by the spirit of his nostrils they are consumed.”

senses.gloss: (dual) face, above all bowed to the ground
senses.definition: The dual אַפַּיִם, “the nostrils”, is the face, chiefly in bowing: to fall or bow “nostrils to the ground” before a king, a lord or God. Once of the face that sweats.

evidence.note: Joseph's brothers “bowed down to him, אַפַּיִם אַרְצָה”.
Lot rose to meet the two angels “and bowed down, אַפַּיִם אַרְצָה”.
Joseph “bowed down with his face (לְאַפָּיו) to the earth”.
David “fell on his face (לְאַפָּיו) to the ground, and bowed three times”.
Abigail “fell before David (לְאַפֵּי דָוִד) on her face (עַל־פָּנֶיהָ)”: אַפַּיִם beside פָּנִים.
The woman of Tekoa “fell on her face (עַל־אַפֶּיהָ) to the ground and bowed”.
Bathsheba “bowed, אַפַּיִם אֶרֶץ”, to King David.
When fire came down on the house, all Israel “bowed אַפַּיִם אַרְצָה on the pavement and worshipped”.
The people “bowed and worshipped Yahweh with their faces (אַפַּיִם) to the ground”.
Kings and queens “shall bow down to you, אַפַּיִם אֶרֶץ, and lick the dust of your feet”.
“In the sweat of your face (אַפֶּיךָ) you shall eat bread, until you return to the ground.”
The New Testament's same act: “falling on his face (Peshitta עַל אַפַּוהי) he will worship God.”
The elders “fell on their faces (Peshitta עַל אַפַּיהוֹן) and worshipped God”.

senses.definition: Anger, as the hot, snorting breath of the nose. Above all the anger of Yahweh against sin, “kindled”, “burning” and “turning back”; also the anger of men. The phrase חָרָה אַף “the nose burned” is the common way to say a man or God was angry.

evidence.note: “וַיִּחַר־אַף יַעֲקֹב against Rachel, and he said, Am I in the place of God?”
When Potiphar heard his wife's words, “his nose burned”.
Judah: “Let not your nose burn against your servant.”
Moses saw the calf and the dancing, “and the nose of Moses burned”, and he broke the tablets.
“Yahweh heard, וַיִּחַר אַפּוֹ, and the fire of Yahweh burned among them”.
“The nose of Yahweh burned against Moses.”
“The nose of God burned because he went, and the angel of Yahweh stood in the way as an adversary (לְשָׂטָן) to him.”
“Cursed be their אַף, for it was fierce, and their wrath (עֶבְרָתָם), for it was cruel.”
“Until your brother's אַף turns from you and he forgets what you did to him.”
“Yahweh, do not rebuke me in your אַף, nor discipline me in your heat (בַּחֲמָתְךָ).”
“A soft answer turns away heat, but a hurtful word stirs up אַף.”
“Make no friendship with a בַּעַל אַף, a master of anger.”
Of the kings who set themselves against Yahweh and his anointed: “Then he will speak to them in his anger (בְאַפּוֹ) and terrify them in his fury.”
“For his אַף is a moment, in his favour (בִּרְצוֹנוֹ) is life”: anger set against favour.
“Though you were angry (אָנַפְתָּ) with me, your אַף turns back and you comfort me”: noun and verb together.
“He, being compassionate, covered iniquity … many times he turned back his אַף.”
“He does not hold fast his אַף for ever, because he delights in covenant love.”
“I will heal their turning back, I will love them freely, for my אַף has turned from him.”
“The אַף of Yahweh will not turn back until he has done … the purposes of his heart; in the latter days you will understand it.”
“I trod them in my אַף and trampled them in my heat, and their juice spattered on my garments.”
“On the day when Gog comes against the land of Israel … my heat will come up in my nose (בְּאַפִּי).”

“Before the burning of the anger of Yahweh comes on you, before the day of the anger of Yahweh comes … seek Yahweh, all the humble of the earth … perhaps you will be hidden in the day of the anger of Yahweh.”
Yahweh did not remember his footstool “in the day of his אַף”.

senses.gloss: long of nostrils: slow to anger, patient
senses.definition: אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, “long of nostrils”, is one whose anger is slow to come: said first of Yahweh in the proclamation of his name, then of the wise man. Its opposite is “short of nostrils”, quick-tempered.

evidence.note: Yahweh proclaims his name: “Yahweh, Yahweh, a God compassionate and gracious, אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, and abounding in covenant love and truth.”
Moses pleads the same words after the spies.
Jonah: “I knew that you are a gracious and compassionate God, אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם, and relenting from harm.”
“Return to Yahweh your God, for he is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger.”
“Yahweh is slow to anger and great in power, and he will by no means clear the guilty”: patience is not acquittal.
“You are a God of forgiveness, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger … and did not forsake them.”
“For my name's sake I make my anger long (אַאֲרִיךְ אַפִּי) … that I may not cut you off.”
“A man's discretion makes his אַף long, and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.”
“One slow to anger has great understanding, but one short of spirit exalts folly.”
“Better one slow to anger than a mighty man, and one who rules his spirit than one who takes a city.”
“A man of heat stirs up strife, but one slow to anger quiets contention.”
“By length of nostrils a ruler is persuaded.”
The opposite: “One short of nostrils (קְצַר־אַפַּיִם) acts foolishly.”

evidence.locator: Psa.2.5, בְאַפּוֹ → ἐν ὀργῇ; Psa.110.5, אַפּוֹ → ὀργῆς; Zep.2.3 → ὀργῆς; Isa.63.6 → ὀργῇ; ὀργή renders אַף ×82

evidence.note: “Hide us … from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come”: the day of Yahweh's anger of Zep 2:2–3 and Psa 2:12.
“The nations were angry, and your wrath came”: the nations' raging and God's anger of Psa 2:1, 5.
“You are storing up wrath for yourself in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God.”

evidence.locator: Exo.15.8, אַפֶּיךָ → θυμοῦ; Isa.63.3, בְּאַפִּי → θυμῷ; Zep.2.2 → θυμοῦ; θυμός renders אַף ×63

evidence.note: “He treads the winepress of the wine of the fury and the wrath of God the Almighty”: the winepress trodden in anger of Isa 63:3.

evidence.locator: Exo.34.6, אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם → μακρόθυμος; Psa.103.8 → μακρόθυμος; ×10

evidence.note: “Do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and long-suffering (μακροθυμίας), not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?”
“The Lord is not slow about his promise … but is long-suffering (μακροθυμεῖ) toward you, not wishing that any should perish.”
“Count the long-suffering of our Lord as salvation.”
The leper “fell on his face (Peshitta עַל אַפַּוהי) and begged him”.

parallels.note: “Heat”, the commonest partner of אַף: anger as burning.

opposites.note: “Favour”: his anger a moment, his favour a lifetime.

phrases.gloss: the burning of anger, fierce anger

evidence.note: “Turn from the burning of your anger, and relent of the harm to your people.”
Negated: “will not turn back until he has done it”.

phrases.gloss: long of nostrils: slow to anger
nostrils to the ground: bowing low
the day of the anger of Yahweh

evidence.note: “The Lord at your right hand shatters kings in the day of his anger.”

phrases.gloss: master of anger: a hot-tempered man

words.summary: Fourteen times, always of the anger of God against his people or against a man (in Psa 2:12, of the anger of the son). It says in a verb what חָרָה אַף “the nose burned” says with the noun, and the two stand side by side (Isa 12:1, Psa 2:12, Psa 85:6).

senses.definition: To be angry with someone (בְּ), above all of Yahweh with his people when they sin, in prayers that ask how long it will last.

evidence.note: “Kiss the son, lest he be angry (יֶאֱנַף) and you perish in the way, for his anger (אַפּוֹ) is soon kindled.”
“Though אָנַפְתָּ with me, your anger (אַפְּךָ) turns back.”
“Will you be angry (תֶּאֱנַף) with us for ever? Will you draw out your anger (אַפְּךָ) to all generations?”
Solomon's prayer: “if they sin against you, for there is no man who does not sin, and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy”.
“God, you have rejected us, you have broken us; you have been angry; restore us.”
“How long, Yahweh? Will you be angry for ever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?”
“Would you not be angry with us until you had consumed us, with no remnant?”

senses.definition: Always of Yahweh, angry with a man or with Israel, often with “very” and a purpose to destroy.

evidence.note: “Yahweh was angry (הִתְאַנַּף) with me also because of you, saying, You also shall not go in there.”
“Yahweh was angry with me because of your words, and swore that I should not cross the Jordan.”
“At Horeb you provoked Yahweh, וַיִּתְאַנַּף יְהוָה with you to destroy you.”
“Yahweh was very angry with Aaron to destroy him, and I prayed for Aaron also.”
“Yahweh was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned from Yahweh.”
“Yahweh was very angry with Israel and removed them from his sight; none was left but the tribe of Judah.”

evidence.locator: Psa.2.12, יֶאֱנַף → ὀργισθῇ; Isa.12.1, אָנַפְתָּ → ὠργίσθης

evidence.note: “The nations were angry (ὠργίσθησαν), and your wrath came”: Psalm 2 turned back on the nations.

words.summary: Daniel's Aramaic, twice, in the plural with “his”: אַנְפּוֹהִי. It keeps the נ that Hebrew assimilates into the doubled פ of אַפּוֹ.

senses.definition: The face, fallen on in homage, or changed in anger.

evidence.note: “King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face (עַל־אַנְפּוֹהִי) and bowed down to Daniel”: the Aramaic of the Hebrew's “nostrils to the ground”.
“Nebuchadnezzar was filled with heat, and the form of his face (צְלֵם אַנְפּוֹהִי) was changed against Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego”: anger seen in the face.

words.summary: The Peshitta's word for the face, πρόσωπον, a plural in form like the Hebrew dual, with the doubled פ of Hebrew אַפּוֹ. Its idiom נְסַב בַּאפֵּא “take face” is to show partiality, and its participle “takers of face” renders ὑποκριταί.

senses.definition: The face, fallen on in worship or prayer, or changed in appearance.

evidence.note: Jesus “fell on his face (עַל אַפַּוהי) and prayed”.
The disciples “fell on their faces and feared greatly”.
The leper “fell on his face and begged him”.
As he prayed, “the appearance of his face (חֶזוָא דַּאפַּוהי) was changed”.

senses.gloss: take face: show partiality; play a part
senses.definition: נְסַב בַּאפֵּא, to take or regard the face, is to favour persons; “takers of face” are hypocrites, who act for show.

evidence.note: “You do not take the face of men (לָא נָסֵב אַנְתְּ בַּאפֵּא דְּאנָשָׁא)”: for βλέπεις εἰς πρόσωπον ἀνθρώπων.
“As the takers of face (נָסְבַי בַּאפֵּא) do in the synagogues”: for οἱ ὑποκριταί.
“Do not be like the takers of face, sad, for they disfigure their faces.”

words.summary: Twice, in the lists of unclean birds. Which bird is not known: scripture says only that it is unclean and has kinds, and the Syriac and Akkadian bird names of the same consonants do not fix it either. Its link to the root's sense is not understood; nothing in the text ties it to the nose or to anger, though a long or prominent beak (Akkadian appu is also “beak”) is a possible lead.

senses.definition: A bird not to be eaten, listed with the stork, the hoopoe and the bat.

evidence.note: “The stork, הָאֲנָפָה according to its kind, the hoopoe and the bat.”

cognates.gloss: nose; (dual) the two nostrils; ḥamiya ʾanfuhu “his nose grew hot”: he was enraged
cognates.note: The nose as the Hebrew's: the dual is the two nostrils, and Arabic says anger with the same picture, the hot nose, as Hebrew חָרָה אַף.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 116, art. ءنف, أَنْفٌ (n1361)
evidence.note: “The nose … The dual is applied to The two nostrils … حَمِىَ أَنْفُهُ (tropical:) He became vehemently angry, or enraged; as also وَرِمَ أَنْفُهُ.”

cognates.gloss: turn up one's nose at, disdain, scorn; disdain, indignation, anger
cognates.note: A verb from the nose for a feeling, as Hebrew אָנֵף is: in Arabic disdain and indignation, in Hebrew anger.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 115, art. ءنف, أَنَفَهُ (n1357)
evidence.note: “أَنِفَ مِنْهُ … [He turned up his nose at it;] he disdained it; scorned it.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 116, art. ءنف, آنفهُ (n1358)
evidence.note: “He, or it, induced him to feel disdain, scorn, indignation, and anger.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 117, art. ءنف, أَنَفَةٌ (n1368)
evidence.note: “Disdain; scorn … indignation; and anger.”

cognates.note: The verb with its נ, as in Hebrew אָנֵף, and in the same use: a god angry with his land and people, who are then oppressed by an enemy, as in Deu 9:8 and 2Ki 17:18.

evidence.note: עמרי מלך ישראל ויענו את מאב ימן רבן כי יאנף כמש בארצה: Omri king of Israel oppressed Moab many days, for Kemosh was angry with his land.

cognates.note: With the נ assimilated into a doubled p, as in Hebrew אַפּוֹ.

evidence.note: Meanings: nose, beak, tip, extremity, top, peak; 528 instances.

evidence.locator: Reconstruction: Proto-Semitic *ʔanp- “nose, nostril”, descendants: Ge'ez አንፍ (ʾänf)

cognates.note: The Targums' word for the face and the nose; Biblical Aramaic keeps the נ (אַנְפּוֹהִי), the Targums and Syriac assimilate it.

evidence.note: “face, presence”, Targ. Ezk. I, 6.
“nose”, Targ. Lam. IV, 20.

cognates.gloss: a kind of bird: hoopoe, or a large eagle or vulture
cognates.note: A bird name of the same consonants, keeping the נ; the bird it names is uncertain in Syriac too.

evidence.locator: Classical Syriac ܐܢܦܐ, noun (etymology 1): kind of bird: hoopoe; large eagle or vulture

evidence.note: 21 instances, Middle Assyrian to Neo-Babylonian; also in lexical lists (dcclt x0020053).

doctrine.statement: Man was formed of dust, and became a living soul when Yahweh God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life (Gen 2:7). That breath is not a second self: the same words, “the breath of the spirit of life in its nostrils”, are said of every creature, man and beast, that died in the flood (Gen 7:22), and while it is in his nostrils a man lives (Job 27:3). So Isaiah says, “cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for of what account is he?” (Isa 2:22), and Adam was told he would return to the dust he was taken from (Gen 3:19). Scripture gives man no life of his own beyond that borrowed breath. Paul quotes Gen 2:7 and sets beside it “the last Adam, a life-giving spirit” (1Co 15:45): life that does not end is not in the first man's nostrils but is given through Christ, at the resurrection, “those who are Christ's at his coming” (1Co 15:22–23).

When Yahweh proclaimed his name he called himself “long of nostrils”: his anger is slow to come, it lasts a moment where his favour lasts a life, and many times he turned it back (Exo 34:6; Psa 30:6; Psa 78:38; Mic 7:18). But in the same breath he “will by no means clear the guilty” (Exo 34:7; Nam 1:3), and his patience is time given to turn: “the kindness of God leads you to repentance”, while the hard heart stores up “wrath in the day of wrath” (Rom 2:4–5; 2Pe 3:9, 15). That day is the one Psalm 2 foretells: Yahweh sets his king on Zion and speaks to the rebel nations in his anger, and they are told to “kiss the son, lest he be angry” (Psa 2:5–6, 12); the Lord at Yahweh's right hand “shatters kings in the day of his anger” (Psa 110:5). Revelation takes up these words at Christ's coming: the great day of the wrath of the Lamb, when “the nations were angry and your wrath came”, and the kingdoms of the world become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ (Rev 6:16–17; 11:15, 18). The “day of the anger of Yahweh” is a day on earth, and the call before it is Zephaniah's: seek Yahweh, seek righteousness and humility, that you may be hidden in it (Zep 2:2–3).

note: The conjunction אַף “also, even; how much more” (BDB a.ex.aa, Aramaic xa.be.aa; Dan 6:23, Ezr 5:10, 14; 6:5) shares the spelling and the brief counts its tokens under a.em.ab by spelling, but it is left out: it is another root. Evidence: (1) the noun has a נ that shows wherever it is not assimilated, in Biblical Aramaic אַנְפּוֹהִי (Dan 2:46; 3:19), Arabic ʾanf, Ge'ez ʾänf, Moabite יאנף, and as a doubled פ in Hebrew אַפּוֹ, Akkadian appu, Syriac ʾappē; the conjunction never shows either, and in Aramaic and Syriac, which keep the noun's נ or its doubling, the conjunction is plain אַף / ܐܦ (SEDRA files ܐܦ “also” under its own root 181, apart from ܐܦܐ “face”, root 182); (2) no Semitic language has a nose word meaning “also”; Arabic ʾanf has no such use (Lane art. ءنف), while Ugaritic has two separate words ảp, “nose” and “also” (Wiktionary records them as two etymologies), and Phoenician has ʾp “also”. The conjunction needs its own entry, keyed by its own consonants (root אפ, which the database already gives xa.be.aa); gam.json already records it only as a parallel. BDB a.ew.am (“אַף vb, see אנף”, a cross-reference with no tokens) is not claimed. Names: Appaim (1Ch 2:30–31, a.em.ac) is written as names/appaim.json. Harumaph (חֲרוּמַף, Neh 3:10, h.fo.ae) looks like חָרֻם “slit, flat” (Lev 21:18) with אַף, “slit-nosed”; it is filed under חרה in the database and is left for the entry of חרמ, not written here. The Peshitta word ܐܦܐ is written as a word of the entry (lang syc) with no root of its own, since its spelling without נ would join it to the conjunction's key; SEDRA: lexeme 245, AIA (root 182), “face; hypocrite; presence-bread”; lexeme 243, AI (root 181), “also; even”. Leads not followed: Sabaean/Minaean ʾnf “wall, façade” (Wiktionary, as a transferred sense of “nose”), not checked in Biella or SabaWeb; Ugaritic ảp “nose” not checked in Segert or DULAT; Ge'ez ʾänf not checked in Dillmann or Leslau. The bird אֲנָפָה: its identity (heron is the common guess) rests on nothing in scripture; no tie to “nose” or “anger” is shown. Psalms and Hosea are cited by Hebrew verse numbers (Psa 2:12, 30:6, 85:6, 60:3; Hos 14:5). Ezk 38:18 (Gog's invasion of the land of Israel) is cited under anger as Yahweh's fury in that day. The brief's 409 tokens for a.em.ab include about 130 of the conjunction; the noun's own count is about 275.
